nameStory: These crabs earned their ghostly name from their pale, sand-colored shells that make them nearly invisible against beach sand, and their uncanny ability to vanish in a flash when you approach. Like phantoms of the shore, they seem to materialize out of nowhere at dusk, then disappear back into their sandy burrows at the first sign of danger.
description: Atlantic ghost crabs are medium-sized crabs with pale, sandy-colored shells that perfectly match beach sand. They have long, spindly legs built for quick sprints across the sand, and distinctive stalked eyes that can peek up from their burrows like tiny periscopes. These crabs typically grow to about 2 inches across their shell, with males often slightly larger than females. Unlike many crabs that live in water, ghost crabs spend most of their adult lives on dry land, though they still need to return to the ocean to breed.

idTips.label: Sand-colored camouflage
idTips.description: The shell ranges from pale cream to grayish-tan, perfectly matching the color of dry beach sand - so well that you'll often spot their movement before seeing the crab itself

idTips.label: Square-ish shell
idTips.description: The carapace (top shell) has a distinctly boxy, almost rectangular shape when viewed from above, unlike the more oval shells of many other crabs

idTips.label: Stalked eyes
idTips.description: Two prominent eyes sit on moveable stalks that can swivel independently, often the only part visible when they're peeking out of burrows

idTips.label: Long running legs
idTips.description: Four pairs of long, thin legs built for speed - they feel surprisingly delicate if you gently handle one, like thin twigs

idTips.label: Burrow holes
idTips.description: Round holes in sand about 1-2 inches across, often with small sand pellets scattered nearby - the entrance to their underground homes

habitat: Look for Atlantic ghost crabs on sandy ocean beaches from the high tide line up into the dunes, particularly in areas with fine, dry sand that's easy for them to dig. They prefer beaches with gentle slopes rather than steep drop-offs, and you'll find their burrows scattered across the upper beach zone that only gets wet during storm surges. In New England, they're most common on Cape Cod beaches and islands like Martha's Vineyard and Nantucket.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging from deeper winter burrows as temperatures warm, though they're still sluggish in cool weather. Look for fresh burrow holes appearing in the sand.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity time - ghost crabs are most active at dawn and dusk, scurrying across beaches to feed. This is the best time to observe their behavior and spot them outside their burrows.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to dig deeper burrows for winter. Young crabs that hatched earlier in the year are now large enough to spot easily on the beach.
seasonality.winter: Mostly dormant in deep burrows below the frost line, though you might spot the occasional individual on warm days. Burrow entrances are often plugged with sand.

funFact: Ghost crabs can run up to 10 miles per hour - making them one of the fastest land crabs in the world - and they run on their tiptoes using only four of their eight legs, holding the other four up like a sprinter's arms for balance.
confusionNotes: The holes in sand might be confused with those made by beach fleas or other burrowing creatures, but ghost crab burrows are perfectly round, about the size of a quarter to half-dollar, and usually have small pellets of excavated sand nearby. Remember: "Ghost holes are round and neat, with sand balls at your feet."
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "Atlantic" ghost crabs, they actually spend most of their adult lives on land and can drown if kept underwater too long - they've evolved special gills that work in air. They only return to the ocean's edge to mate and release eggs.
compareHints: Atlantic ghost crabs are the only ghost crab species found in New England waters, making identification straightforward within their genus. They can be distinguished from fiddler crabs (their closest relatives in the area) by their pale coloration, more rectangular shell shape, and habitat preference for dry sand rather than muddy marshes. Unlike fiddler crabs, ghost crabs don't have one dramatically oversized claw.
